doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Pilobolus and dance collaboration
summary: Working with Pilobolus and Richard Bull's dance company led to her interest in sound and movement.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I forgot to ask you about your Pilobolus. That must have been fun, huh?

Well I met the Pilobolus Company in 1979 when I lived in New Haven and they worked out of Connecticut. So one of the dancers, Allison Chase, became aware of my work and she wanted a solo saxophone score for her new solo piece that she had done, it was later called “Moonblind.” So we spent a lot of weeks working in her studio. I loved it. And I didn’t realize at the time how much I loved modern dance and working with dancers. And as time moved on, when I got to New York, I started working with an improvisational dance company, which was run by a choreographer named Richard Bull. And I spent many years performing with them, not only as a player but learning how to play and move at the same time with the improvisational dancers. It was some very bold stuff. And I think again it was kind of like an experience that I jumped off from, learning about playing and moving and why I’m interested in how sound changes when it moves, and not being afraid of the physical aspect of myself as a player, kind of becoming more conscious of it, more aware of it, more interested in it. Because the dancers were fascinated with it. Musicians might go huh, but the dancers were just fascinated and they helped me you know. So over time my work with Pilobolus, I did the “Moonblind” piece for them early on, late 70s, and a couple of years ago I orchestrated a piece for the full company called “The Doubling Cube” which they’re now performing on tour all over the world, so it’s on tape and it has a lot of drums and saxophone and bass on it too, as well as some electronic sounds.
It must be a thrill to write something that has some longevity to it like that, that goes out and is spread around.

Yeah. Well that’s how you think about records too. You know you don’t realize what a life they have after you’ve given birth to them. They go out into the world and affect people in ways you never know, sometimes not until 15 years later.
